Pour améliorer l’accès aux lunettes de v: To improve access to prescription glasses for immigrants without status, Le Bonhomme à lunettes makes the rounds of community organizations in Montréal.
<strong>Popularisées par les plus grande: Popularized by the biggest luxury brands as a fashion accessory in its own right, eyewear can reach astronomical prices. To improve access to what remains an essential health device, including for people without status, Le Bonhomme à lunettes has been making regular rounds of Montréal community organizations for 17 years. Our report.
Dans le hall de Fourchettes de l’espoir,: In the lobby of Fourchettes de l’espoir, a social economy enterprise in Montréal-Nord, two opticians with dozens of pairs of glasses neatly arranged in their cases advise their customers. “We come here every Wednesday from 1 to 3 p.m.; anyone can come, you just need a prescription,” says Mathieu, one of the 25 opticians employed by Le Bonhomme à lunettes.
Un peu plus loin, plusieurs personnes at: A little farther along, several people wait patiently for their turn while new customers join the line. In one hour, about ten of them have chosen or picked up their pair. But why do they all come here rather than going to a traditional optical store?
Rondes ou rectangulaires, noires ou colo: Round or rectangular, black or colourful, metal or plastic, all these glasses leave customers facing an almost impossible choice. The young man trying on pairs doesn’t seem to know where to look. Fortunately, his aunt is with him, giving advice. She’s the one who told him about Le Bonhomme à lunettes.
« Je suis mère de trois enfants, dont de: “I’m a mother of three children, two of whom wear glasses, and I wear glasses myself. I come here because it costs me half as much! Especially since kids tend to lose them or break them, so it was a significant budget item every year. With inflation, I’d rather keep that money for something else. So I realized I had to find an alternative. Ever since I first set foot here, three years ago, I haven’t gone anywhere else,” says Aïcha, a teacher of Moroccan origin who has lived in Montréal-Nord for more than a quarter century.
Le Bonhomme à lunettes lui permet d’écon: Le Bonhomme à lunettes allows her to save several hundred dollars every year, which her family can put toward other essential needs, such as groceries, clothing and extracurricular activities.
D’autant que Aïcha ne bénéficie pas, com: All the more so because Aïcha does not have group health insurance, as many Montrealers do. “As teachers, the government system doesn’t allow us to have health insurance, and RAMQ coverage is clearly insufficient for the prices asked in traditional stores. Here, the opticians don’t try to sell us the most expensive pair or options we don’t need,” says the woman in her fifties. Thanks to her, her nephew will pay only about a hundred dollars, compared with the $300 spent on his previous frames.
Dany est elle aussi enseignante. Avec sa: Dany is also a teacher. With her blond hair falling elegantly over her shoulders, her stylish glasses on her nose and freckles on her cheeks, she looks much younger than her age. Approaching retirement, she is also a regular at Le Bonhomme à lunettes.
« L’été, quand l’école est fermée, je to: “In the summer, when school is closed, I go on unemployment. So I’m careful with my money, I check the flyers, I compare prices… Before, I paid at least $650 for a pair of progressive glasses, here it’s $300! Clearly, that’s the kind of savings that will let me enjoy my summer despite everything,” says the woman, who has lived in Montréal-Nord for 10 years.
À l’heure où se loger n’a jamais coûté a: At a time when housing has never been so expensive and finding a job is increasingly difficult, getting medical care has become a luxury for a growing share of the population. This is especially true of vision and dental care, which are among the most poorly covered.
<strong>Personnes sans statut, bénéficia: People without status, social assistance recipients: pairs from $0 to $20
Placer les lunettes de vue à la portée d: Putting eyeglasses within reach of every budget has been the credo of Le Bonhomme à lunettes since its founding in 2007. While it serves everyone, it targets people in precarious situations in particular. Among them, immigrants without status are among those most at risk of going without glasses because of a lack of money or information.
« Pour les bénéficiaires de l’aide socia: “For social assistance recipients, we offer free glasses for children and $20 pairs for adults. Of course, if they want special options, like lenses that darken or anything else, that raises the bill,” says Mathieu, one of the two opticians present that day in the lobby of Fourchettes de l’espoir.
Mathieu, opticien au Bonhomme à lunettes: Mathieu, an optician with Le Bonhomme à lunettes, shows dozens of pairs of glasses to customers at Fourchettes de l'espoir. (Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy)
Le programme Mieux voir pour réussir, de: The Mieux voir pour réussir program of the Régie de l’assurance maladie du Québec (RAMQ) also offers a $300 reimbursement every two years on glasses or contact lenses for all young people under 18. “With the prices we charge, that lets each child have three pairs instead of one, or lets parents keep the rest of the money for other expenses,” says Philippe Rochette happily.
S’étant fixé pour objectif de toucher to: Having set itself the goal of reaching all populations, Le Bonhomme à lunettes also visits organizations that work with immigrants. “For refugees or asylum seekers, all we need is the famous ‘brown paper’ [the name given to the refugee protection claimant document (RPCD), Editor’s note] to give them access to federal assistance. That way, we can offer them fully covered glasses,” he explains.
« On offre les mêmes services que dans l: “We offer the same services as traditional stores, the difference being that we’re mobile and we have a community mission. ‘Mobile’ means we travel with our rolling store to 75 service points in Montréal and the surrounding area. The other important difference is that we have no sales targets, unlike what I experienced elsewhere as an optician. We simply look for what will be best suited to each person’s needs,” says Mathieu.
C’est cet aspect communautaire qui perme: It’s this community aspect that allows the man in his thirties to “feel useful and bring meaning” to the heart of his work. There are 25 opticians who have chosen, like Mathieu, to join this enterprise unlike any other. Because, contrary to what one might think, Le Bonhomme à lunettes is not officially a community organization. It is very much a for-profit company.
<strong>Plus de 150 000 $ versés aux act: More than $150,000 paid to community groups every year
« J’avais envie de trouver une façon d’u: “I wanted to find a way to use my qualifications as an optician to help others.” As you will have gathered, Philippe Rochette is not a businessman like the others. He made the unusual choice not to adopt a strategy based on the race for profit. Seventeen years after founding Le Bonhomme à lunettes, he has met the challenge with flying colours.
Derrière un regard vert lagon qu’aucune: Behind lagoon-green eyes that no pair of glasses conceals is a 49-year-old Montrealer, father of two young daughters to whom he wants to pass on his values.
Philippe Rochette est le fondateur et di: Philippe Rochette is the founder and head of Le Bonhomme à lunettes. (Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy)
« Je suis né dans une famille monoparent: “I was born into a single-parent family, with a father who left my mother, my sister and me penniless. Today, I have the luxury of being able to make a very good living from my work while staying true to my values. That’s also, I think, what my employees like, whom I pay well and who have no sales targets. I have a very good retention rate,” he says. But how does he manage to offer such prices while still turning a profit?
Il n’y a aucune recette miracle, Philipp: There is no miracle recipe: Philippe Rochette has cut every expense. The hundreds of pairs of glasses offered to customers follow current trends, but none is designer. No luxury brands here. “I did everything on my own for the first four years, and since 2007 I’ve always charged the same prices, inflation or not. We go to organizations that lend us their space, so we have no rent. We don’t do advertising or marketing either, and we negotiate volume with suppliers. It’s no more complicated than that, and it works!” says the business owner enthusiastically.
Opticien diplômé, passionné de cinéma et: A certified optician, film buff and tennis fan, Philippe Rochette has always volunteered. To carry his idea through, he also donates part of his profits to the 75 community organizations that host the service points. Since its founding, Le Bonhomme à lunettes has given nearly $1.5 million to the community sector, or about $150,000 every year. Funds that are more than welcome when you consider how increasingly difficult it is for these essential groups to secure grants.
« C’est un système gagnant-gagnant ! Auj: “It’s a win-win system! Today, it’s the organizations that ask us to come to them,” concludes Philippe Rochette. Here is proof, if any were needed, that on the margins of capitalism, the social economy is capable of setting off a virtuous circle.
